# Background {#sec-background}

## Physical activity and health

The relationship between activity volume and health outcomes is generally
curvilinear: the largest relative gains occur when the least active become
moderately active [@bauman2012]. Beyond a certain volume the curve flattens,
so the public health argument for reaching *some* activity is stronger than
the argument for reaching a lot.

Observational studies consistently report lower all-cause mortality among
active adults, but they are vulnerable to reverse causation: people who are
already unwell move less. Randomised trials avoid that problem at the cost of
shorter follow-up and smaller samples.

## Training responses in older adults

Ageing is accompanied by a decline in maximal oxygen uptake of roughly 10% per
decade after the age of 30. Supervised endurance training can offset part of
this decline, and the relative improvement in older adults is comparable to
that seen in younger populations, even if the absolute values remain lower
[@garber2011].

Three mechanisms are usually invoked. Central adaptations increase stroke
volume and cardiac output. Peripheral adaptations increase capillary density
and mitochondrial content in the trained muscle. Behavioural adaptations —
simply moving more outside the sessions — contribute an amount that is rarely
measured.

### Individual variation

Responses to a fixed training dose vary substantially between individuals.
This variation is partly measurement error and partly genuine biological
heterogeneity, and separating the two requires either repeated baseline
measurements or a control group followed over the same period.

Studies that have done so suggest that true non-response to endurance training
is rare once the delivered dose is verified. Apparent non-response is more
often a matter of adherence than of biology.

### Dose and adherence

Supervision matters because it makes the delivered dose knowable. In
unsupervised programmes, the difference between the prescribed and the
completed dose is frequently the largest single source of variation in the
outcome.

## Cardiometabolic outcomes

Changes in blood pressure, fasting glucose and waist circumference following
endurance training are typically small in absolute terms. They are, however,
consistent in direction, and at a population level even a 2–3 mmHg reduction in
systolic blood pressure is meaningful.

## Summary

The literature supports a benefit of structured training, but few studies have
followed community-dwelling older adults under supervision for a full 12 weeks
while also verifying the delivered dose. That gap motivates the present work.
